title: Walt and Roy Disney: Dreamer and Banker
text:
Roy Disney was eight years older than his brother Walt. In 1923, when Walt arrived in Los Angeles with almost nothing after his first animation company in Kansas City went bankrupt, Roy was there recovering from tuberculosis. In October that year the two founded the Disney Brothers Studio. Walt supplied the ideas and the drive; Roy handled the money, the contracts and the banks.

The pattern held for forty years. When Walt decided to make a full-length animated feature, Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, the industry called it Disney's folly, and costs ran far over budget. Roy went to the banks again and again to keep the project alive. It opened in 1937 and was a huge success. When Walt dreamed up Disneyland in the 1950s, Roy at first doubted it, then found the financing, partly through a deal with a television network.

The brothers argued often and fiercely, and at times barely spoke. Yet each knew he needed the other.

Walt died in December 1966. Roy, already in his seventies and planning to retire, stayed on to build Walt's last project, a vast resort in Florida. He insisted it be called Walt Disney World, so that people would always know it was his brother's dream. It opened in October 1971. Roy died two months later.
lesson: One person dreams and another makes it possible, and both are needed. Disagreeing fiercely does not have to break a partnership built on respect.
location: Los Angeles, California, and Orlando, Florida, USA
source: Neal Gabler, Walt Disney: The Triumph of the American Imagination (2006); Bob Thomas, Building a Company: Roy O. Disney (1998)
